speechtext:

Press reports and press releases have indicated that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) was in Manila just over a month ago discussing the international financial situation, with particular reference to currency flows, with IMF and World Bank officials. subsubtopic: PROPOSED ACTION TO SECURE RELIGIOUS FREEDOM IN SOVIET UNION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that Christians and other religious believers in the Soviet Union are being persecuted simply because they desire to worship God according to the dictates of their conscience and the precepts of their faith rather than according to the dictates of the state; and in view of the fact that a symbol of the denial of basic human rights by the Soviet Union is the imprisonment for five years at hard labour of Georgi Vins, Secretary for the Council for the Evangelical Christians and Baptists, for the alleged crime of administering to the congregation that elected him as their pastor, and the continuing persecution of the Vins family, which for three generations has suffered imprisonment and death, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway):
That members of this House urge the Prime Minister to make representation to the government of the U.S.S.R. that Georgi Vins be released from imprisonment and that the government of the Soviet Union allow him and all other religious believers within its borders to worship God freely according to their own consciences, as the Soviet Union is committed to do by the provisions of its constitution and by the provisions of the United Nations Covenant on Civil and Political Rights which the Soviet Union has ratified.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. In prefacing my usual business question today, I wish to say that the official opposition is delighted with the announcement that the Acting Prime Minister made today with regard to the introduction of the Independence of Parliament Act, particularly in view of the fact that government members rejected a motion which would have allowed a study of this subject earlier in the week, the motion having been made by a member of the official opposition.
Dealing with the matter of the legislative program, I ask the House leader to inform the House of the business that he contemplates for the balance of this week and perhaps next week. Is the House leader prepared to make a statement today with regard to the arrangements concerning Remembrance Day, and with respect to Friday, November 12? There have been some discussions on that. In addition, will he designate on the order paper the opposition days which he and I have discussed and which I understand are in order, subject to certain caveats which he wishes to make.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be able to deal with all the points raised by the hon. member. On the first question with regard to the regular business of the House, we will continue with the borrowers and depositors act. If it is necessary to complete the business of a particular day, we will call the Currency and Exchange Act and the Canada Land Surveys Act. However, at the beginning of the next full day I will call the government expenditure restraint bill. On Tuesday next it is my intention to have an allotted day. For planning purposes, I wish to indicate to the House that the following are proposed as allotted days in addition to November 9: November 18, November 26, December 1 and December 9.
With regard to the sittings of the House next week, as hon. members know, Thursday of next week is Remembrance Day and is, accordingly, a day when members are in their constituencies. In order to make the proper arrangements for next week, it is my proposal that we not sit on the Friday following Remembrance Day and, in order to pick up some time, that we sit for an extra two hours on Tuesday, November 16. If these
Business of the House
arrangements are agreeable to hon. members I am ready to propose a motion that will put them into effect. I shall read the motion and then ask for consent. I propose to move:
That when the House adjourns on November 10, 1976, it shall stand adjourned to November 15, 1976; and that the House shall sit from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. on November 16, 1976, for the purpose of considering government business.
If I have consent, I will move that motion.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in continuing the debate on Bill C-16 let me say at once that since the bill was introduced a few days ago there has been considerable criticism of the poor manner in which this measure has been drafted. Consumers and lenders have listed complaints with regard to the proposals before us. They have drawn attention to inequities in those proposals. Once again we are being asked to deal with legislation which has been drafted in the absence of proper consultation with the borrowers and the lenders organizations.
The government would like us to hasten the debate on the various bills which are brought forward, but there is no way in which we in the opposition will agree merely to rubber-stamp pieces of legislation which have not been properly drafted and with respect to which the legitimate interests of those con-


cerned have not been taken into account. The Canadian Bankers Association considers it uncomplimentary to banks to have them and other legitimate financial institutions lumped together with loan sharks under the borrowers protection bill. This matter was mentioned yesterday.
Loan-sharking, Mr. Speaker, has nothing to do with the bill before us. Loan sharks form part of the criminal element and should be dealt with by the police. Mr. Frazee, who is the executive vice-president and chief general manager of the Royal Bank of Canada, feels the government, in seeking to achieve the commendable object of ensuring that the consumer is protected against unscrupulous lenders, has gone overboard in introducing legislation which covers all financial institutions. He also warned that if increased costs for legitimate lenders were involved in meeting the provisions of the bill, everybody, including consumers, would end up suffering.
Referring to the view of the government that because they have computers financial institutions should find no problem meeting the provisions of the bill, including the provision which specifies that interest shall be calculated and credited daily on deposit accounts, Mr. Frazee pointed out that all financial institutions are not fully computerized-the Royal Bank is not, for example-and that these provisions would mean employing increased personnel.
In addition, Mr. Frazee objects strongly to what he sees as an assertion in the bill that a lender is guilty until proved innocent. This is a reference to the unwarranted rate concept: the bill allows a borrower who believes he is being overcharged to stop payment on a loan or to apply to the court for a review of the credit charges. In case of such dispute, the onus would be on the lender to prove that the rate charged reflected only the normal cost of lending money and the risk presented by the borrower. Mr. Frazee suggested that this provision might allow some unscrupulous borrowers to take advantage of lenders. Another aspect of this bill to which Mr. Frazee objects is the one which prescribes that lenders must state a single effective credit charge for each loan. Included in that charge would be interest, insurance charges, brokerage fees and charges for appraisals, investigations and credit reports.
The views I have put on the record are examples of the criticisms which this poorly-prepared piece of legislation has been receiving. I can see we shall have our work cut out in committee before we are finished with the legislation. In all probability, the bill will have to be completely rewritten, and this would be just another useless and unnecessary delay in the operation of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday during my speech on Bill C-16 I stated that to solve the problem of loan-sharking and excessive interest rates the minister was proposing to set a legal ceiling on interest rates. That legal ceiling would be seven times the present prime rate; in other words, the legal ceiling
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors that the minister intended to have would amount to between 70 and 75 per cent.
The minister challenged me on this, and I replied that I had read this information in press releases from the minister's office, that I had heard it said by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), by Conservative members and by one of my colleagues. The minister then rose on a point of order. I might say that when I said I had heard of it from one of my colleagues, the minister said that I had given a false impression. Therefore, I told the minister that after my speech 1 would check my notes to see where I had found the formula that the minister was proposing, and if I was mistaken and it was not in any of his releases, I would apologize to him.
I have checked my notes and the press releases, Mr. Speaker, and it certainly is not in the minister's press releases or in his speech. Therefore, I should like to apologize to the minister for making that statement. However, I should like to tell the House where I did get that statement and probably where Conservative members and the Liberal member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) and my colleague from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) got it. They got it from a letter that was sent to the minister by the Consumers' Association of Canada, dated October 20, 1976. 1 checked with the Consumers' Association of Canada who informed me they had obtained that information from a presentation contained in legislative proposals prepared by the minister's department for a convention in Ottawa of federal and provincial consumer and corporate affairs ministers. The proposal was used for discussion purposes on December 1, 1975.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the CAC said they had an interview with the minister and his officials, and their letter of October 20 relates to those interviews. At that time the unwarranted rate was mentioned-in other words, the rate between 70 and 75 per cent, anything in excess of that being a criminal rate. They did discuss it with the minister and his officials and the minister did not deny it. As a result, the Consumers' Association of Canada wrote to the minister setting forth their views in that regard.
To further strengthen my contention in regard to the formula of seven times the basic rate, namely, between 70 and 75 per cent, and any interest charge over 75 per cent being a criminal rate, I checked with provincial ministers. I was advised that officials of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs have advised officials in provincial departments of consumer and corporate affairs that this was the rate intended to be used by the minister with regard to the regulations he hopes to present to the committee.
In these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, although I have apologized to the minister for making a mistake by saying the information came from his press releases, I think he has been unfair not only to me but also to the hon. member for Windsor West, to Conservative members and certainly to my colleague for Timiskaming, and he owes it to the House to clarify the matter and to state categorically what the unwarranted rate and the criminal rate will be. It is not sufficient that he wait until we get to committee stage when he can present his


Protection of Borrowers and Depositors regulations. The least he can do is to be fair to members of the Elouse and tell them at this time. Otherwise, I think he has been unfair to me in challenging where I obtained that information.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before commencing my remarks I wish to congratulate the minister on his appointment from the backbenches. Being just two years in the House, he will realize that anything I say derogatory of the bill-because I really do not have much good to say about it-is nothing personal. 1 find it rather astounding, as one who still accepts the fact that there is a supernatural order and that there can still be miracles; but this is a new kind of miracle, that a minister can be appointed and within a month bring in legislation. It must have been churning through the bureaucracy. I get a great kick when I read legislation like this and realize that some are opposed to the decentralization policies of this government. For goodness sake, if this is the kind of efficiency that exists in the bureaucracy in Ottawa, it is no wonder the country is facing such terrible economic obstacles. I do not want to make a blanket condemnation, of course, because this would be quite unfair to many dedicated civil servants in various offices. Nevertheless, it seems to me obvious that one case of incredible inefficiency on the part of swollen bureaucracy in Ottawa is evidenced by the provisions of Bill C-16.
The minister says the bill is long overdue. That is one of the great understatements of this parliament. The minister has pointed out that under the British North America Act the subject of interest falls within federal jurisdiction, and he was frank enough to admit that existing legislation was hopelessly out of date. The fact that the Small Loans Act has not been amended for 20 years says a good deal about the way this country has been governed, and its economy managed, by recent Liberal governments.
The minister knows that since 1946 the total consumer debt of this country has increased from roughly $1 billion to more than $23 billion. As he noted, more than 65 per cent of that increase has occurred since 1967. In the period 1947 to 1975, non-mortgaged debt has increased three times as much as disposable income. Again I repeat that this says something for this and past Liberal administrations which have been so snail-like in attempting to make an honest commitment to protect borrowers from the inadequacies of present institutional arrangements between borrowers and lenders.
In light of spiralling increases in consumer debt in this country during the last 15 years, and the increasing publicity given to the maldistribution of income that exists, it is amazing
[Mr. Gilbert.) *
that we have taken so long to give adequate credit protection to the working and non-working poor, or at least to consider reforms in existing legislation. One would have thought that, given the fact that Great Britain, the United States and the most progressive European countries in the last 15 years introduced the type of legislation that is before us in this bill, this would long ago have spurred this government to come up with meaningful protection for low income borrowers, as they promised so fervently during the 1974 election campaign. It has taken them 2Vi years to get where we are now, Mr. Speaker. A lot of time will be spent in committee mending this legislation before I, for one-and, I think my party-will consider voting for it.
Since this legislation is designed, presumably, to protect those who are suffering from the persistent and continuing maldistribution of the national income, it might be well to remind ourselves of the seriousness of this disease which we seem to find so difficult to face. The widespread inequity in the distribution of the economic pie is suggested in a comparison of the figures issued by Statistics Canada for the period 1965 to 1974 which relate to the distribution of income by income groups. The percentage of total income received by family units-which is defined as including families and unattached individuals-between 1965 and 1974, for the bottom 20 per cent compared to the top 20 per cent, reveals the following: in 1965 the bottom 20 per cent received 4.4 per cent of the total economic pie, and in 1974 they received 4 per cent. While the top 20 per cent received 41.4 per cent in 1965, by 1974 they received 42.5 per cent. The sad part is that both in Canada and the United States the relative position of these groups has been the same since 1951, despite the increase in all the individual components that go to make up the welfare state in a mixed capitalistic system.
If we consider the distribution of income by income group and do not include family units which take in unattached individuals but only families, we find that the bottom 20 per cent earned less than $3,320 in 1965, and the top 20 per cent earned more than $8,944. In 1974 the bottom 20 per cent earned less than $7,480, while the top 20 per cent earned more than $20,174. The total income received by these families in 1965 was 6.2 per cent for the bottom 20 per cent, while in 1974 they received 6.3 per cent: In 1965 the top 20 per cent received 39 per cent, and in 1974 they received 38.8 per cent. According to Statistics Canada, in 1974 there were 5.5 million families in Canada and 93,500 families received less than $3,000 a year.
Some people claim that these statistics need to be qualified. It is pointed out, for instance, that the lowest income group who get such a teeny-weeny morsel of the economic pie are not a permanent group, but change from generation to generation. In the parlance of economists, they are a flow and not a stock. This takes nothing away from the argument that the lowest 20 per cent, made up largely of senior citizens and single women who are heads of households, suffer badly in our economic system. It is also pointed out that these figures make no


allowance for income "in kind", such as medicare and low-cost drugs for elderly citizens. But the very rich also receive the benefit of medicare, old age pensions, etc. Since we are talking about the relative positions of income groups, this fact has also to be considered. It is difficult for anybody to rationalize the curious and ugly symmetry which characterizes income distribution in Canada.
The report of the Senate committee on poverty which was published in 1971 showed that one of the major causes of low income, or poverty, was that regressive taxes such as sales, excise and property taxes, fall more heavily on these unfortunate groups. In other words, the effect of the income tax system which is progressive-that is, based on the ability to pay-is cancelled by the low income groups paying a proportionately higher share of these taxes that are not based on ability to pay. We all know that tax loopholes and shelters favour the high income groups in our society. We will be more specific on this matter later, Mr. Speaker.
In the debate on the Speech from the Throne, the leader of our party pointed out that under the registered retirement savings plan a tax shelter allowed those earning $25,000 or more to stash away $1,502 in 1974, while those in the $5,000 to $10,000 income bracket only saved an average of $34 under the same scheme. This party, in season and out of season, has stressed the unfairness of our total tax system.
In the 1972 election campaign we pointed out that the rich and the very large corporations were receiving income welfare payments and subsidies from the Liberal government through inequities in the tax system. We were told this was socialist propaganda. We pointed out that all kinds of hidden subsidies were being given to the large corporations and the upper income groups in our society. We were accused of pandering to the lazy by trying to correct some of these gross abuses through such things as a guaranteed income for the working poor and the non-working poor. It always struck us, and still does, as being somewhat paradoxical and odd that when the country gives such breaks to the large corporations and the wealthy, it is considered either a grant or an incentive to save; but when transfers are suggested for the lower income groups, we are criticized for pandering to the welfare bums.
Just yesterday the National Council of Welfare, scarcely a socialistic organization, brought additional conclusive evidence and confirmation of what we in this party have been claiming for a very long time. The council found that Canada's hidden welfare system allows the federal government to transfer billions of dollars to wealthy taxpayers through inequitable income tax deductions and exemptions. Some examples of existing inequities cited in the report are as follows. Someone earning $30,000 per year saves $62 in income tax for contributing $135 to the Canada Pension Plan, while someone earning $9,000 per year and contributing the same amount saves only $37. A woman earning $6,000 per year claims the $1,000 child-care deduction, thus reducing her taxable income for a tax saving of $257, while a woman earning $20,000 applies the same deduction, for a saving of $380. A person earning between $5,000 and $10,000 per year places $1,000 in
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors a registered home ownership savings plan and receives a grant or tax saving of $264.93, while the person earning between $15,000 and $20,000 saves $365.80 under the same plan.
The council, which is a government-financed advisory body for the Department of National Health and Welfare, maintains that average taxpayers, the middle and low income wage earners, are unaware of the mechanics of the Income Tax Act. It is also clear that it is they who bear the greatest burden of the costs I have mentioned, while it is the wealthy who reap the greatest benefits.
I have engaged in this preamble concerning income distribution and the inequalities of the tax system because I wanted the bill which we are debating on second reading to be put in the context of the political and economic realities of some of the major problems which face Canada today. It is unfortunate that the proposed legislation did not take these facts into account. Instead, Bill C-16 had its origin, as I noted before, during the 1974 election campaign. At that time, in an effort to obtain a majority government, the Liberals brought forward legislative proposals-but I note that most of these promises have not been kept after I'h years. The Liberals have never felt compelled to live up to their rhetorical flourishes on the campaign trail. F. R. Scott's closing couplet dedicated to Mackenzie King continues to apply to them: "Do nothing by halves which can be done by quarters". As Scott suggests, the Liberals do manage to bring forward bits of good legislation, however reluctantly.
One of the positive changes in this legislation, which has been noted by many speakers, includes standardization in respect of banks and financial institutions calculating interest rates on savings accounts. Presently, deposit institutions have a form of windfall profit because of their method of calculating interest. Interest charges will be figured on an annual basis and must be paid on the net principal sum, and will be calculated for savings purposes on the average, rather than the minimum amount in savings. The amount that the borrower will actually get in his pocket will be the basis of calculation, rather than the present system which includes administrative and other costs.
Third, we have the government's belated recognition that there is such a thing as a criminal rate of interest. Presently there arc no controls on the amount of interest some moneylenders can squeeze out of their desperate customers. As the minister noted in his speech, the loan shark racket has become, according to police sources, a $3 billion a year business in Canada. I, for one, have great reluctance in accepting that figure. I wish the minister would note, as he finds his way in his new ministry, that Statistics Canada should be pushed to come up with some reliable figures. Dependence upon police force figures in respect of loan-sharking seems to be an incredible, inefficient and questionable procedure. I very much doubt there is a business in illegal loan-sharking in Canada to the amount of $3 billion a year.

Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
Of course, if we include some of the loan-sharking which goes on in the finance companies we could easily come up with a figure of $3 billion. But in speaking of an underworld type of thing, as I believe is implied in the use of that figure, it strikes me that it is ridiculous. On this question, the minister also used statistics that were corrected by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) who mentioned that the minister had said that in the order of $296 million was lent in 1974 under the Small Loans Act with protection under the $1,500 loan level. As the hon. member for Windsor West pointed out, it is really more than $400 million that we are talking about.
In talking about this whole question of loan-sharking, whether legal or otherwise, the minister did not mention the measure of responsibility the government should accept for having allowed this situation to exist for so long. The fourth thing, in general, that is pretty good about this bill is that fixed rate mortgages will be brought into line with the present practice in respect of NHA mortgages. This measure is long overdue. It will allow up to 10 per cent of the outstanding principal to be paid on the first or second anniversary of the loan or on any payment after the third anniversary. All or part of the outstanding principal can be repaid, with the maximum penalty being three months' interest on the amount prepaid.
I thought it was kind of a joke, as I read some of the speeches, to find there were those who were so concerned that the "poor" trust companies and finance companies might lose in these transactions with the poor. The important thing is to help them become more competitive and to allow consumers to use the sovereignty that is supposed to be theirs under a competitive market system. Some members seem to be protesting against this, in favour of giving more protection to the lender instead of more freedom to the borrower, and therefore more competition among those who are lending.
That is what the private enterprise system is supposed to be all about. There must be controls on advertising, so that rates and conditions of credit will be prominent in the ads. There are some people among our party, and probably some among the backbenchers in all parties, who would like to see a total ban on credit advertising, but I think it has to be at least strongly regulated because one can often look in vain for the information aspects which are supposed to be the best part of advertising. So much of it is just waste.
We already know that one of the greatest weaknesses of the capitalist system, whether or not it is a mixed capital system, is the huge waste inherent in the economic institution called advertising, where we have in North America, I think, somewhere close to $30 billion a year now invested in that industry. It is very difficult, even for the most avid defender of that system, to say that most of that really contributes to the common good of the people in our countries. I know it is extremely difficult to regulate the informational component as compared to the other, but we must remember that the criticisms that are being made about the poor and low income people in respect of unemployment insurance, going after too much credit and all these types of things, relate to the values that are being created by the media which depend upon these

advertising revenues. They would ask the poor to turn themselves off and close their ears to this sort of thing because it is only geared to those who can afford it.
These are the cultural values and the cultural consequences of the system that is being defended here all the time by many spokesmen from the old-line parties. It is just like the criticisms that are made in respect of the poor blacks in the United States when they want cars or coloured television sets, and so on. Why should they not want these things, when they are being pushed by everything in that society to want them, and when the measure of value of the people in that society is so often the possession of material goods, money, and so on. What an insult to human beings! These represent either the cultural contradictions or the consequences of that system which must be faced. One is being hypercritical when one tries to blame the low income groups for so much that is society's own responsibility for what is really a cultural conditioning process. I do not say it is a deterministic one, but it is a cultural conditioning process which so many people in our society, including those who speak for the defenders of the capitalist system in the two major parties in this House, do not seem to want to recognize or take seriously.
To get back to the bill, Mr. Speaker, there are new disclosure rules in all credit transactions to standardize the formula for presenting such information so that it will be easily comparable. Of course, that is a step in the right direction. Finally, the administrator must enforce the act and advise the public of their rights under the act. In many ways, the success of the act will pivot on the terms of reference given to the administrator and, of course, the actual choice of the administrator. It is essential that an activist person, with legitimate and credible credentials, be chosen for this position. Let us hope that patronage will not play a predominent role in the choice of an administrator by a new minister who is trying to establish some credibility. The work which his department embraces is becoming a more and more important part of people's welfare in our society and it is desperately important that the right people are appointed at the top. This is what the bill proposes, and while I applaud many of the individual initiatives, the general thrust of the bill seems, to me, to leave much to be desired.
The first principle, establishing the fact that there is a criminal or usurious rate, is a breakthrough. Thomas Aquinas wrote about this, and I am glad hon. members on the other side have discovered this theologian who lived in the twelfth century. The Liberals have finally caught up with Aristotle and Aquinas, these men of history. But this principle must be coupled with other measures.
Any sincere effort to protect consumers from loan sharks and their criminal rates of interest must come to terms with the reasons people deal with loan sharks in the first place. Quite simply, financial institutions are unwilling to give some people loans because of the high risk they represent. The government should implement a comprehensive insurance


scheme for small consumer loans along the lines of the Canada student loan plan. When 1 was campaigning in 1974, I listened to the Liberal platform and sometimes said to myself that what they said was so good that it was too good to be true. In fact, now we find that it was so good that they did not even legislate it. Not only have they done this tremendous flip-flop on wage and price controls, as it is known in the country, but they did not even legislate the good things they were saying.
When they finally got around to legislating it 2'h years later, they neglected to put into legislation one of the principal things they offered to the Canadian people. That insurance idea was a tremendous selling point to the middle income group and low wage earners which, coupled with the promise not to freeze prices and wages, is in my opinion, largely responsible for the fact that the Liberal party is now in government. They promised this insurance scheme, and now they are not even offering it. Why is the government so scared of including an insurance scheme in this legislation along the lines, for example, of the Canada student loan plan? This would have a twofold effect. First, since banks and other financial institutions would be guaranteed payment-and we have nothing against that-interest rates charged to high-risk customers would no longer be justified. In reference to this point, I might add that the vast majority of high-risk loans, as has been repeated in the House several times, are repaid on schedule, thus creating no problem to the lending institutions. You can verify this by asking any credit union manager: he will confirm it. Thus you have the paradox of these institutions getting the highest return on loans to people who can least afford to pay it. Second, if these loans were guaranteed, the poor in many metropolitan areas-and the minister should recognize this better than someone like myself-would not be forced to turn to loan sharks, especially the illegal ones, but could deal with the legitimate lending institutions.
With this loan insurance scheme the criminal rate of interest could be set at a substantially lower rate than now envisaged, because the reason given for high interest rates by the legitimate store-front loan sharks-and they might not like to be called that, but in my experience even some of the respectable finance companies advertising in our media can be so called- is the risks involved. While it is true that there is a largely criminal element involved in loan-sharking, in my experience-and, I think, in the experience of many others-some of these finance companies can be rough on borrowers. Some hon. members seemed to be surprised at some of the things the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) mentioned about a certain individual who was forced to pay back his loan to a well known finance company. Coming from a mining town, I saw such things as furniture being removed from houses because people could not pay back their loans.
Of course, those finance companies have been engaging in a loud public relations campaign in recent years, saying that they have changed their methods and practices. Perhaps they have, but certainly they have left traumatic memories, aversion and resentment in those of us who saw some of their actions. So it seems to me no coincidence when we see in some
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors of the hard-hit, low income areas, such as the one I represent, the only new activity in the commercial centres of the various towns consisting of the opening of more and more finance companies. These companies may not be the sharks or barracudas mentioned by the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), but they sometimes remind me of vultures circling around a wounded animal, waiting to take advantage of the helpless victim. They advertise low monthly repayment schemes, but always play down the bottom line. The actual interest rate charged by the so-called good corporate citizens-only filling a need in society-often exceeds 24 per cent. It is vital that the government set clearly within this bill the maximum rate of interest that can legally be charged, rather than through regulation later. I was glad to hear my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), making the point he did, and I think correctly, to the minister today. As a social democrat-

It is vital that the government set the maximum rate of interest that can legally be charged clearly within this bill, rather than through regulations later. As a socialist, I would like to see the maximum interest rate allowable set at an extremely low level, but this cannot be done in isolation and, given the existing economic system, it is not possible. However, even given our present mixed capitalist economy, outlawing interest rates above 24 per cent would be feasible. The minister will be surprised at how many of his own backbenchers agree with that.
Now 1 would like to return to the matter of the role of the administrator in overseeing this legislation. His office has great potential, but his powers would have to be enlarged. As the legislation reads now, the borrower must initiate, through default, any action against the finance company. As the minister knows from experience-we come from different economic backgrounds, but surely he has had enough experience with low income people, or if he has not, surely the people who are advising him or some of his friends can tell him-these people will not take IAC or Household Finance to court. It is a clear misunderstanding of the way lower income people think, and ignorance which shows how scared they are of these institutions. My goodness, I run into people in my constituency who are scared of going inside a bank, let alone a courtroom.
The matter of going to a court was raised by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray). The responsibility of taking corporations of large size to court strikes me as dreamy stuff. Most people do not want to be dragged into court by lending institutions, for any reason. In this regard the government is putting the cart before the horse. These people should

be able to appeal to an ombudsman. As the bill now stands, borrowers must renege on their loans and face court action to prove that the interest rates they have been charged are excessive. Does the government believe that people will use this type of mechanism to demonstrate that interest rates are excessive? If the minister thinks so, he is not in contact with the people that I am. I repeat, to most Canadians, being taken to court is a traumatic experience. There is a stigma attached to people who are taken to court. 1 do not foresee many hard working Canadians defaulting and then facing giant lending companies in courtrooms.
I suggest that borrowers should be able to turn to the office of the administrator-and I see his role as that of an ombudsman, which I would prefer him to be called. I think that is a Swedish term, and the Swedish people have made much more use of ombudsmen than we have. I think that is a good concept. Ombudsmen have a good image; administrators have not. Administrators are considered bureaucrats-and the AIB has not helped that, either. I see the administrator's role as that of an ombudsman who would have both the regional staff and the resolve to look into these matters.
The government has also decided to abolish the ceiling on interest rates on small loans under $1,500. The $1,500 level may be set too low, given the inflation we have been experiencing. This level should be raised to, perhaps, $3,500 or $4,000, but the ceiling on interest should not be removed. The minister should think about that and try to get some more advice on this matter. I just cannot understand some of the thinking of the people who prepared this legislation. The hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane) tried to defend this type of thing.

speechtext:
If the minister does not like what I am saying, he should read the speech of the hon. member for Windsor West. It may be argued by some that lenders will not make money available for small loans if a ceiling is placed on the interest rate. I am sure that is what the minister is talking about. This may well be true, but it seems to me that it can very easily be corrected by this government ordering lenders to make available a reasonable percentage of their lending capital to small loans. That does not seem to be an awfully difficult demand in order to help low income groups.
The government talks a lot about disclosure of all information relating to the true cost of loans, such as insurance, administration costs, et cetera. This is well and good, but the borrower should have all the information. The lender should have to tell his prospective customer his credit rating and how he arrived at the interest rate charged.
This bill tries to come to grips with the problem of the lack of consumer understanding of the credit system, but it falls short. The government should embark on an extensive adult
|Mr. Hogan.]
education program to make Canadians aware of their rights and responsibilities. Credit counselling could be done by setting up offices where they are needed. An important function would be to dissuade people from borrowing for things they cannot afford. That will be hard to do, considering that every day on television we are told to buy, buy, buy-and to buy on credit. People could be counselled to put off buying until they are in better financial shape. This education program could be handled by some non-governmental group such as the Consumers' Association of Canada. In addition, individual credit counselling could be carried out through local offices of the ombudsman and institutions delegated by him to perform this function. The ombudsman would thus oversee the legislation.
One of the things I like is the idea of data bank collection which is mentioned in this bill. I suggest to the minister that that will only give us more details about the use of consumer credit, but besides making this information generally available to business firms it could be an important source of information for government policy-making. Although this is not directly related to the bill, the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) issued a caveat about invasion of privacy. I think that is a good point. His notion is very sound and I think the Department of Finance should use the data as a tool of policy in order to make a better diagnosis of consumer intentions.

speechtext:
Bill C-16 was drawn up with the best intentions, but the substance is not there. I get the feeling that the people in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs are completely out of touch with the people they are trying to help.
In his opening remarks, the minister said that Canadian banks are some of the largest and best run in the world, and that other lending institutions serve effectively and honestly the credit needs of Canadians. He neglected to add that they are also some of the most profitable. But for whom are they best run? Why is there a $1 billion to $3 billion per year loan shark racket? Why does that exist if lending institutions serve the public so well? The truth of the matter is that banks and other lending institutions have failed to provide the type of service Canadians have a right to expect.
In spite of the extravagant "Have you got a dream" advertising campaign of the Bank of Montreal and its assertion that it is there to help Canadians grow, the ultimate thing the Bank of Montreal, or any other bank, is interested in is the bottom line. With this in mind, if the government is serious about helping Canadians with their credit problems, careful and thorough regulation of these giant lending institutions is needed through this act and the upcoming changes in the Bank Act.



In summary, the government must face the fact that until a basic redistribution of income is achieved in Canadian society, all the tinkering of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will come to naught. This bill could be a basis for Canadians to get a better deal from moneylenders and credit institutions, but only if the legislation is changed drastically in committee. First, the role of the administrator must be expanded to that of an ombudsman. He, or she,-not the courts-must have the power to rule on excessive interest rates charged to borrowers. That office must vigorously inform Canadians of their rights under this legislation. The rate of interest which would be classified as criminal must be set at a realistic level, somewhere between 24 per cent and 33 per cent per annum. The illegal loan sharks can be completely put out of business by proper licensing procedures. In committee, I hope the government will see the error of its ways and keep the ceiling for small loans.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would first like to thank and congratulate all those who took part in the debate on Bill C-16, especially my colleagues on this side of the House. I offer my sincere congratulations to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) who had the courage to introduce this very sensible bill.
This bill is of great importance for Canadians, especially the less fortunate who are often victims of unscrupulous money lenders who are usually called loan sharks or underworld bosses. In my humble opinion, this is one of the most popular bills to be introduced; it had been expected and prepared for two years, and my colleague the Hon. Andre Ouellet, worked very hard on it when he was Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I would like to pay him tribute for the great work he did concerning this bill.
The Liberal party accepts members who do not necessarily share our opinions. The hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) proved this in his speech when he criticized and approved in principle the bill now before the House.
Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief. I shall make only a few comments so as not to delay passage of this bill. Therefore, if I may, I shall speak in general terms.

Mr. Speaker, I am full of enthusiasm about Bill C-16 now being debated in the House. The bill is, I believe, right and ripe, it having been introduced at the proper time when Canadians across the land have been asking for such protection. It is a bill with teeth, a bill with which everybody agrees in principle.

Why this bill? The federal government has the firm intention of protecting the Canadian consumer. Consumer credit has more than doubled since 1967 and has now reached over $24 billion, not including mortgages. Let me explain: The bill
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors also grants important rights to real estate owners who want to reduce their interests by prepaying their mortgages. Essentially, this is an improvement over traditional mortgage loans offered under the National Housing Act.
Other provisions will help consumers who take out a variable rate mortgage. The present legislation is outdated. The Small Loans Act was amended for the last time in 1956. This bill will rectify the situation. The complaints we are receiving show that, from a consumer's viewpoint, credit problems are among the most important. The government wants to make the rules of the game consistent and to simplify them as much as possible. The increase in loan shark activities calls for strong government action. Loan sharking has become organized crime's second main industry. According to police estimations, that racket is now getting over $3 billion in Canada.
What does the legislation in the way of protecting consumers? The bill will clarify credit rules by establishing uniform methods of computing interest, by forcing lenders to clearly disclose the terms of a loan, and by regulating credit advertising in every form. The bill will give increased protection to the borrowing consumer, by giving him more legal remedies, by allowing him to repay his debt at any time without penalty, except in the case of mortgages where penalties will be significantly reduced, by putting the burden on the lender to prove his case if things come to an end, and by limiting lender recourses for debt collection.
Any Canadian who has to risk his credit is entitled to a minimum of protection, just as the millions of people who try to lay their savings to advantage. This legislation will therefore provide and effective tool to fight loan sharking and establish a criminal rate beyond which any lender will face severe penalties ranging from $1,000 to $10,000 fines or up to years imprisonment, or both. The consumer will therefore get his money's worth. It is the federal government's duty to control unfair interest practices. We are determine to rid Canada of all loan sharking activities. There will be a legislation to help the consumer get a loan at a reasonable rate. Police forces will have legal means at their disposal to fight that terrible disease. Also, the onus of proof will rest with loan sharks and illegal lenders. Every lender will be forced to disclose the terms and conditions of the contract. Loans sharks who cash ahead of time family allowances cheques, social insurance or income tax cheques are profiteers who charge interest rates from 400 per cent to 1500 per cent to those poor victims. For loan sharks, it is the second biggest source of income. The first one being prostitution and the third, drug trafficking. This bill is aimed at eliminating intimidation and black mail.
This bill is not only concerned with lending transactions entered by trust or banking institutions. This government is also interested in the activities of every dealer, those who sell goods and services on credit, ranging from national or multinational enterprises to local car, clothes or furniture dealers.
The reign of the loan sharks is coming to an end. With the cooperation of the opposition parties we hope to see this bill through in the shortest time possible and we are ready to


Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
accept constructive suggestions. 1 have no doubt that the opposition will not demonstrate a mean and partisan attitude.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that Bill C-16 that we are presently studying is extremely necessary for a very important number of Canadians who borrow or deposit money in the banks.
I agree with the minister when he says that the chartered banks are considered as the most important and better organized banks in the world and that, furthermore, some other credit institutions efficiently cater to the financial needs of all Canadians. But what 1 want to know is this: What is the rate of interest, what will be the costs to the borrower? It is quite clear that, pursuant to the British North America Act, the federal government has jurisdiction when it comes to interest rates and that any transaction made with an interest falls within the purview of the central government because when looking at the British North America Act, and especially at subsections (2), (3), (14), (15), (19) of clause 91, one can notice that the central government has all powers when it comes to trade and commerce, the raising of money by any mode or system of taxation, banks and the issue of paper money and, what we are particularly interested in, interest rates.
When he introduced the bill, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs declared, I quote:
The Interest Act was last amended in 1917. The Small Loans Act has not been amended for 20 years. In the last 30 years alone, total consumer debt-not including mortgage debt-has increased from less than $1 billion to more than $23 billion. More than 65 per cent of that increase has occurred since 1967. Today, excluding mortgages, consumer debt represents more than 22 per cent of our total disposable personal income. In the period from 1947 until 1975, non-mortgage debt has increased fully three times as quickly as income.
Mr. Speaker, when I read such figures, I cannot help thinking of unwarranted interest rates which are, in my opinion, the major cause of inflation in Canada and also of the prodigious escalation of Canadian consumer indebtedness as a whole. To correct this situation, the government has decided to introduce a very timely piece of legislation which, in its view, will help relieve market conditions and stimulate competition in such an important sector as consumer credit. I respectfully suggest, even though 1 support the bill, that if this government wishes to help the consumer, it should take the necessary steps to reduce interest rates and cut off incentives to loan sharks.
Mr. Speaker, consumers are going into debt to maintain, if not to increase, their standard of living and often to get out of

financial straits. To appreciate this, one only has to take a quick look at the last figures available, that is for June 30, 1976.
Canadian indebtedness represented the impressive amount of $20,263 million, an increase of 17.3 per cent over a year ago.
Curiously, one could read in the daily Le Soleil of September 24 last, and 1 quote:
It should be noted that chartered banks are the greatest credit dispensers with two thirds of the total. Personal loans as of July 30 last stood at $14,841 million, 23.7 per cent more than a year ago.
On the other hand, personal cash loans made by lending and finance companies represent a small percentage of the overall credit; they are even down slightly for the period under review. According to official statistics those loans stood at $1,773 million a year earlier.
As to credit extended by those same institutions to finance consumer purchases it accounted for a slightly higher volume at the same date, $1,143 million compared with $1,138 million a year ago.
That is not all, Mr. Speaker. Canadians are borrowing more than ever on life insurance policies. Up to the month of August 1976 loans on life insurance policies stood at $1,202 million, an increase of 6.8 per cent, and outstanding credit at $1,186 million exceeds by even $100 million the credit obtained in department stores. I sincerely think that the rise in interest levels that we witnessed in recent years and even today is simply due for a large part, of course, to our institutional structures because there is no doubt that our financial institutions exercise and have exercised considerable influence on rising interest rates.
In January 1924 at the general shareholders meeting of the Midland Bank of London, Mr. Reginald McKenna, president of that bank and also former British Chancellor of Exchequer, had this to say:
1 am afraid the average citizen would not like to be told that banks can
Note what he is saying.
-and that is what they do-create and destroy money (credit). The amount of money in existence varies only through the action of banks increasing or reducing their deposits or banking purchases. Any loan, overdraft or purchase by the bank creates a deposit; and any reimbursement of a loan, an overdraft or a sale destroys a deposit.
So this can be summed up this way, Mr. Speaker:
Every bank loan creates a deposit and every repayment of a bank loan destroys it. In addition, it is a well known fact that through the leverage given to them by Canadian legislation, the chartered banks manage to lend, while maintaining a low statutory margin, up to 16 times the amount of this margin, thus creating a new purchasing power. The same banks have acquired those privileges of creating credit out of nothing and of charging a penalty under the form of interest to the borrower, simply because they have every power to create the money required to achieve their aims.
Obviously, this enables us to compare such procedures with the honest behaviour of a citizen who buys government savings bonds available to chartered banks. It simply happens that the poor fellow who has worked hard to save a few pennies invests his few savings, while the banks secure a powerful financial control over the government thanks to the money created


through a manipulation of the banking system. Besides, among all sectors of society, the banks are the only ones which create their means of payment out of nothing. Therefore, it is fair to say that the methods used by the banks to get hold of our country and of the Canadian people are nothing but sheer fraud.
Mr. Speaker, 1 really think that high interest rates are inflationary since they result in higher costs for those who are able to obtain funds and follow the average increase in the cost of living index. In other words, interest rates adjust to inflation and, as a result, interest rates go up along with other costs, just as labour unions claim that wage increases do not preceed rising prices but rather simply proceed from them. As far as I am concerned, I think labour unions are justified in demanding wage increases in view of the ever rising cost of living.
So, I tend to believe that higher interest rates produce exactly the same effects. Frankly, it is easy to admit that everyone is in debt, that all governments, provincial, municipal and federal are hopelessly in debt, and that those debts, because of the millions of dollars paid in interest every year, can only add to inflationary pressures. As we know, that interest is paid by the taxpayers through their taxes. Taxpayers do not print money and so they have to ask for higher incomes and ever increasing salaries to meet cost requirements. All those taxes are finally included in prices because that is the only way producers can recoup higher costs.
The consumer, in an attempt to make up the taxes deducted from his paycheque, through pay deductions, and just like the producers, demand ever higher salaries and wages. One can therefore readily conclude that higher taxes, because of the interest governments at all levels have to pay, a.e reflected in consumer prices and, as a result, add to the growth of inflation.
Mr. Speaker, the statistics quoted previously prove that all Canadian taxpayers suffer from inflation, that worldwide plague, and increasingly higher interest rates. Add to this, of course, our governments. In this regard, former Bank of Canada governor Louis Rasminsky, in a brief presented on July 3, 1969 to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, said, as reported on page 2749 of Issue 55 of its Minutes and Proceedings, and I quote:
One of the casualties of a prolonged period of inflation is the market for long-term debt obligations. This is because investors become increasingly reluctant to commit their funds in such a form even at progressively higher interest rate levels. Private corporations who wish to raise long-term funds can try to combat this trend by offering equity participation, often in the form of convertible debentures, but this option is not open to governments-federal, provincial or municipal-or to home buyers or to publicly-owned utilities who must rely on debt financing to cover their borrowing requirements. It is social capital formation rather than private capital formation which must bear the brunt of the harm done to the long-term capital market by inflation.
Mr. Speaker, before closing this brief statement, I would like to draw your attention to the subject of credit cards.
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
In the Journal de Montreal of November 3, 1976, there is on page 10 an article entitled as follows: "Explosive Danger". Here is what is says:
What would you say if an individual stole your pay every month and asserted in all seriousness that he was doing you a service? You would simply say: He is nothing but a thief. But it is true. Hundreds of thousands of Quebecers are so treated each month and they applaud. You know as well as I do no one is as shrewd as a banker to pocket his neighbour's money. But one day, one of those money men-I don t know who, unfortunately-had a strike of genius, the credit card. I give them a credit card that allows me to lend them money at a higher rate still and I bet ten to one that they will all applaud.
And our poor man was right. Who does not go around without his little plastic card? This genius of a banker had just sparked a revolution in the world of credit and consumer behaviour. In the imaginary museum of the consumer, this inventor should be put on a throne in the best room. The dream was limitless, except for the nightmare. Here is what does happen. You are idly walking around the stores with your little card in your pocket, and with no particular purpose in mind. All of a sudden, without any warning, you are overwhelmed with a tremendous desire for possession while standing in front of something which is useless more often than not, and lo and behold, you buy saying to yourself that you will arrange to have the payments made over 12 or 24 months.
You have just borrowed from the bank which issued your credit card, at a 18 percent interest rate. This is why bankers are terribly pleased when you refer to credit cards. If you have something important or essential to purchase and you do not have the cash for it, why not go to your credit union or your bank where interest rates fluctuate around 14 percent. This way, you are not using your credit card and you will be saving at least 4 percent interest.
Mr. Speaker, this is the plain truth, is it not? Bank credit is simply created by a mere stroke of the pen under a legislative authorization. At any rate, one may conclude that the government instead of being a servant of the people is forced to become their oppressor because of the pressure from financial institution. Admittedly, this kind of situation may tend to have serious consequences on the stability of our economy.
The government has just now realized that Canadians are relying on him to draw the abscess which has been actually undermining the economic health of our society for so long; whether you like it or not, the active forces in our society are increasingly becoming mere robots for the consumer public. As a matter of fact, beyond the limits set by a legislation which is no longer adequately protecting and defending the consumer and which is finally becoming obsolete there are open fields of activity in want of development.
Mr. Speaker, the same goes when it comes to buying, selling or financing new and second hand cars because, if my information is correct, there is hardly any control over this production and consumption sector which is spreading in the international market. Just think about pressure selling best exemplified by hawking which results in misrepresentations and breaches of trust, and God knows what else. One only needs to go to large stores to realize how easily credit is obtained through budget plans and credit cards. From all this one may conclude that publicity leads the dance and Satan calls the tune.
In my opinion, it is high time the government denounced the inadequacy and obsolescence of the legislation which is completely outdated because of the well-organized invasion of mass production which subjects the consumer to the law of the jungle. The government should promote the drafting of a fair, just and clear legislation based on the needs of today's consumers. I also believe it is high time the government saw to it


Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
to establish some protection and defence organizations for those consumers who are unfortunate enough to become the victims of loan sharking and exploitation. And what is more comical about the whole matter is that all this is sometimes legalized and consumption is encouraged through the creation of needs by artificial means most of the time. Moreover, a solution might be for the government to try and establish popular schools in order to convey to consumers of all ages, both indidually and collectively, some basic information as a first means of defence, thus giving the legislation a role of rehabilitation and prevention.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to direct a few remarks to this bill primarily because I did not have the opportunity earlier to congratulate the new minister upon his appointment. I feel a certain kinship with the minister because of the fact that we were both elected in 1974, and because at some time in the past we each sat in the official gallery of the House as executive assistants. I understand some of the exasperation the hon. gentleman may feel, coming into parliament and trying to put into action some of the advice he has been giving over past years.
I wish to draw attention to a few points of interest to me with respect to this legislation. The bill before us has been promised for a considerable period of time, and 1 compliment the government for finally having brought forward the new piece of legislation designed to give borrowers some protection against excessive charges and interest rates. I have personally been interested for some time in updating federal law in this area, and on earlier occasions since 1 was elected I have urged the government to take action in this regard.
It is worth-while noting that the bill before us repeals the interest Act, an insignificant piece of legislation in some respect. I recall, shortly after I graduated from law school, my principal in the law office in which I articled talking to me about conveyancing and mortgages and calling to my attention one of the law's provisions which, I imagine, is very little known. Nevertheless, it is a provision which a lot of people who have mortgages on their homes might like to consider because the effect of it is that unless the mortgage states that the computation of interest is to be made either yearly or half-yearly, and not in advance, then the interest requirement is not enforceable.
I have never heard of anyone bringing an action to seek a declaration that interest payable under a mortgage loan might not be payable because the particular provision of the Interest Act to which I have referred was not complied with, but I wonder whether the minister has it in mind that, on the basis of the precedent established in the Interest Act, interest might not be payable should there be a breach of the legislation he is proposing.
Those who read Hansard might have an opportunity of reading their own mortgage documents and ascertaining whether the wording referred to in the Interest Act is actually contained in such documents. They may then look at the Interest Act and get in touch with their legal counsel with
[Mr. Allard.)
regard to the obligation to pay interest under their respective mortgages. That advice is my little service today to the individual who has a mortgage against his property-and it is something that very few people are aware of.
There are also some other aspects that might be considered in this kind of legislation. I do not know whether the minister would be receptive to specific suggestions for amendments, but one amendment I have in mind might be more drastic than he is contemplating. Coming from Saskatchewan, I can say that the history of the province is such that with it's boom and bust cycle after the great depression, there has been legislation passed which, in effect, puts limitations on remedies available to mortgagees and persons who lend money on the security of real or personal property, which leads me to think out loud, so to speak, that there is room for a similar kind of provision in legislation such as that presented to the House today.
Specifically, I am referring to the kind of provision existing in many provincial jurisdictions in regard to residences or homes, where there is a limitation placed on the remedy available to persons lending money on the security of a mortgage. In many provincial jurisdictions a person lending money on such security is limited to realizing the security itself. In other words, if I were selling a house for $50,000 and received a downpayment of $5,000, and the balance of $45,000 was in the form of a mortgage against the house, in the event of default, in many provinces a limitation is placed on the lender in that he can only realize on the security to the extent of the amount realized on the sale of the house under foreclosure proceedings, whether the sale realized the balance owing of $45,000 or not.
Since the federal government is deeply and heavily committed in the mortgage loan field, it seems not an unreasonable proposition, to me at least, that we consider the following. Wherever a mortgage is used as the basis of security on a home, we might give consideration to limiting the remedy of institutions under federal jurisdiction to the extent of their security under the mortgage as opposed to a right that involves a dual remedy that the mortgagor has to have a judicial sale and then to sue the borrower for any deficiency in amount after the house is sold and the proceeds applied to the balance of the mortgage.
If this legislation is to be regarded as social legislation, we should also consider federal responsibility in the house building and home ownership field. It seems to me that that principle might apply not only to the home itself but to the furnishings. Here, again, there could be a limitation on the remedy of a person who lends money on the security of, say a refrigerator, stove or furniture. Such remedy would be restricted to repossession and realization of that security.
I think there is a good deal to be said in support of the proposition that, aside from the interest rate provision and the attempt to limit the interest charges, consideration should also be given, in the case of institutions under federal jurisdiction, to some sort of limitation of the right of the lender and his


remedy vis-a-vis the home owner, the person buying a home. I think there would be great support for such provisions, not only because the government would then demonstrate its interest in the encouragement of home ownership, but also it would give many home owners some protection. 1 think the minister would agree it would include many young people, such as newly married people who need some sort of protection during the first years of life. I commend some of these ideas to the minister with a view to seeing whether or not the government is interested in extending the protection afforded borrowers and consumers in the two areas I have mentioned.
I also think the federal government is to be commended on coming forward with this legislation even at this late date. Quite frankly, I think the federal government has lagged behind many provinces in this field. Perhaps this is understandable, in view of the fact that the provinces have jurisdiction over property and civil rights and are more directly concerned with this kind of legislation. However, it seems to me that the federal government is now becoming greatly involved in the area of consumer borrowing. In addition, NHA has assumed dimensions of great importance in this country, and CMHC has grown from very modest proportions as originally introduced by the Liberal government in the fifties. Under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when prime minister, the National Housing Act came into its own and a substantial amount of money was made available for home building, which was given real impetus by the government of that day.
I said I would not take too much time, Mr. Speaker, but I do want to commend the government for bringing in legislation to deal with the growing and rather questionable businesses involved in making advances on income tax refunds and welfare cheques. I have written to the minister's predecessors in office regarding constituency complaints about this sort of thing which, quite frankly, feeds on the poor and on people not able to protect themselves. I would be the first to commend the minister on bringing forth this kind of provision and seeing that it is carried out. I do not want to be too negative or critical in my remarks on the bill, and this is one area in which I congratulate the minister and regarding which he will have my full support. This is an insidious practice that goes on in our larger cities, though in many medium-sized cities as well.
One other aspect of the bill on which I want to ask the minister a question, and on which he can possibly elaborate during the course of committee debate, has to do with the absence in the bill of any provision giving consumers access to their credit rating file and their concurrent right to correct any errors on it. We never really know what collection agencies or credit agencies are saying about us. As a friend of mine once said of me-almost anything you could say about me is probably true and I would not have any recourse. On the other hand I am sure my colleagues in this House, most of them being honourable gentlemen, share my concern that information picked up by collection agencies or credit agencies might have very serious consequences in respect of one's ability to obtain necessary financing. That seems to be a not unreason-
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
able proposition and in accordance with at least the apparent undertaking for openness in government mentioned in the Speech from the Throne.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
My colleague, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) questions if it is an undertaking. We are a little apprehensive about the undertakings of this government, Mr. Speaker, but they did mention that they are changing their course and in future will be more open with the Canadian public. I agree with that. If they carry out this undertaking, they will receive their just reward.
In this legislation there is room for provision that any consumer who wishes would have the right to obtain copies of information on file with respect to him, and would have the concurrent right to correct any errors therein. The other aspect of the bill which concerns me is the prohibition on unwarranted interest rates. The bill does not specify any ceiling for interest rates. That will, presumably, be left to the discretion of the minister. This opens up another question that concerns me, because in my observation this government has a propensity for introducing legislation inevitably containing a provision that regulations can be brought forward by order in council to give effect to the act. I hope the minister will not succumb to this tendency to govern by regulation.
I have noticed in my time in this House that some of the most important legislation to be presented has come in the form of bills with perhaps 10, 20 or 30 clauses, the main one providing that the governor in council may make regulations to give effect to the legislation. An example is the Anti-Inflation Act. The only provision of any consequence in the bill gave the cabinet power to move by regulation as opposed to having the details of the governing law outlined in the statute. I abhor this tendency, Mr. Speaker and I am sorry to see that a similar provision exists in the legislation before us. It is appalling how often the government attempts to move by regulation rather than by legislation which is open to the scrutiny of parliament and the public. This should not continue, and it will not after 1978 when I am sure this party will form the government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill should be viewed as an accompanying bill to Bill C-18 which is "an act to ratify the Bretton Woods Agreements." Taking the two together there is, of course, a great deal to say about them. The Currency and Exchange Act, which is before us now, has the simpler background. I can tell the House that the minister will be piloting the Bretton Woods Agreements measure, Bill C-18, and will have considerably more to say about it.
The main purpose of Bill C-5 is to make Canadian legislation with respect to currencies and official international reserves consonant with the amended articles of agreement of the International Monetary Fund. At the same time we are taking advantage of the occasion to introduce a few other amendments of a technical nature.
The amendments before us will give legal sanction to the use of the special drawing right and similar composite units of account in Canadian contracts. It will also give authority to the governor in council to specify how values expressed in SDRs, gold, or foreign currencies are to be calculated in terms of Canadian dollars. This latter provision is intended to remove any legal ambiguity which might arise as a result of the changing role of gold and SDRs as units of account.
We are also proposing that the assets of the Exchange Fund Account, which are denominated in SDRs and foreign currencies, should be valued at current exchange rates so that their value in Canadian dollar terms is accurately reflected in the public accounts. At the same time, given the possibility of large but reversible movements in exchange rates, we do not wish to see large, offsetting charges and credits being made to the Consolidated Revenue Fund in consecutive years. Accordingly the amendments provide for a three year averaging period for these valuation changes.
The list of assets eligible for investment by the EFA is being expanded to include government securities in freely usable currencies with a maturity of not more than two years. The EFA would also be empowered to lend its gold holdings.
Finally, at the request of the Auditor General's office, the requirements for the Auditor General's report are being changed slightly to bring them into line with those contained in other legislation.
In sum these amendments are largely technical in nature and are designed primarily to reflect in Canadian law and practice the changes that are taking place in the international monetary system.
