speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), who I see is in the Chamber, will join in this debate before the evening ends. 1 am surprised he did not speak first himself instead of leaving that task to his parliamentary secretary.
I note that in the statement which the parliamentary secretary read the bill was described as a companion piece to the Bretton Woods Agreements bill which will be coming before us later. He said, further, that while there are certain matters of consequence in it, the bill contains a lot of technical features. Mr. Speaker, it is all very well for a parliamentary secretary to come in and read a page and say, in effect "Don't worry, let's get this passed", but I believe that all members, before deciding how they wish to vote, should get these proposals into perspective.
We are dealing here with billions of dollars and I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if they read some of the technical features of the bill every member of the House would be alarmed by what the Minister of Finance is proposing. I shall be dealing with this aspect more fully later, but I would draw the attention of the House in particular to Clause 5. The parliamentary secretary did not even refer to Clause 5, though that clause contemplates taking away from parliament its right to have the Auditor General report directly to the House concerning transactions involving the exchange fund and covered by the act we are being asked to amend. One of the most fundamental rights this parliament has is to preserve the independent position of the Auditor General so he can report as he sees fit to this House.
I should like to take the House through the sequence of events leading up to the point where we are now being asked, in effect, to cut off one more right parliament has to scrutinize the spending and general financial activities of the government. I feel it is time the members of the House stood up and said that they have had enough of the government's tendency to whittle away the few remaining rights that parliament has over the government of the day.
Let me put it in perspective, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps there is no more volatile question in the world today than that of exchange. There is no more volatile financial or economic factor than the changing of world current account balances. For example, let me refer to the Bank of Canada Review which gives the highlights of the OECD's economic outlook in its monthly publication for August of this year. On page 13 of that Review, in table III, you will see the magnitude of current account balances or imbalances at the present time. These figures are truly staggering.
The total OECD deficits in 1976 are going to be $20 billion. I emphasize that 25 per cent of those current account balance deficits are in this country alone. We have the largest single deficit of any OECD nation listed in the Review to which I have referred. In total OECD anticipates a $20 billion deficit for 1976, and of that amount $5 billion is for Canada alone. The United States deficit is $3.5 billion, Japan has a surplus,

France has a deficit of $2.75 billion, Germany has a surplus, Italy has a $2 billion deficit, and the United Kingdom has a $2.5 billion deficit.
Just on that point, Mr. Speaker, how often are we quick to laugh almost at Great Britain's dilemma? But let us not forget that in the current year we are running a current account balance deficit twice the amount estimated by the OECD report. Let us not assume that this is some type of temporary situation. The fact is that the deficit to which I have referred is likely to continue. The Review shows that, based on an annual report, in the first quarter of 1977 the deficit for OECD countries will have risen to $23 billion.
What I am trying to show, Mr. Speaker, is that we are dealing with huge deficit figures in the world today in terms of current account balances. The OPEC countries, the petroleum exporting countries, have a huge surplus of $51 billion contemplated in 1976, and the non-oil producing countries have a deficit of $21 billion. Other countries have a deficit of $13 billion. The world total deficit will be $3 billion. In short, Mr. Speaker, we have a situation where two industrialized nations, Japan and Germany, are in surplus, the largest surplus is among the OPEC nations, and huge deficits are being piled up by all other nations. That is the framework within which we should consider this bill tonight.
Where does Canada fit into all of this? The fact is that Canada will be called upon, indeed, has been called upon, to share in the bailing out of some countries that have run up big deficits. As we know, Great Britain is in a rather serious predicament. The pound has fallen dramatically and Britain has asked the International Monetary Fund to bail her out immediately with a loan of $3.9 billion. After she receives this money, assuming it is granted, it is contemplated that they will ask world nations for a further bail out of $10 billion.
Rather than the Minister of Finance trying to slip this bill through the House tonight, I suggest that he owes the House a full explanation of what is the government's position in relation to bailing out such nations as Great Britain, Italy, or whoever it is who is looking for credit. Once again I point out, as we did earlier today, that the Minister of Finance went to Manila and entered into some private discussions with World Bank and International Monetary Fund officials, but has never come back to the House and made a statement on what he suggested, or negotiated, or given us any type of briefing on what transpired at Manila, and this in spite of the fact that tremendous amounts of money will be required to bail out various countries with currency problems.
Surely this House is entitled to know what the minister is commiting us to at some of these conferences at which he likes to turn up and puff around like a world figure. I have a copy of the speech that the minister made in Manila so let hon. members not simply take my word as to the size of the problem. In his speech the minister said:
-the liquidity of the Fund has dropped to a low level. I must say frankly that I am concerned about the financing of the Fund programs. There may well be difficulties for the Fund in meeting its commitments if more countries do not, as a matter of urgency, make their currencies freely usable for Fund transactions.


The entry into force of new quotas, the economic recovery and the provisions of the amended Articles will all have a beneficial impact on the liquidity of the Fund. But this will take time and will not solve the problem we are facing right now. I would consequently hope that member countries would make appropriate arrangements with the Fund for the free use of their currencies as soon as possible.
Earlier in his address the minister said this:
In the session of the Canadian Parliament which will commence as I return to Ottawa, I intend to introduce the necessary legislation to adopt the amended Articles.
That is, of the International Monetary Fund. In Manila the minister mentioned he was going to introduce legislation, and we have one of the bills before us tonight. Yet we are not even given the courtesy of having the minister stand up and explain, in introducing the first piece of this legislation, what it is he has in mind and what exactly were the commitments that he made on behalf of Canada when he was in Manila. In my view, Mr. Speaker, that is not what this parliament deserves from the Minister of Finance. If commitments are going to be made to help other nations, either through the International Monetary Fund or directly, then we should learn from the government exactly what conditions are going to be attached to such bail outs.
For example, are we going to continue, through the awarding of credit, to bail out, say, Great Britain without saying that we will help them financially only if they agree to pull in their belts and act more responsibly so far as spending is concerned?

Mr. Speaker, to sum up, I simply feel that when the Minister of Finance is dealing with these interrelated subjects-and the two bills are interrelated, the one dealing with Bretton Woods, and this one-it is time he explained to the public and to this House the exact commitment he is entering into in some of these international forums. More and more we are being committed to bail out other countries. The time is fast approaching when we have to say to nations such as Great Britain that no further credit is available until they put their own house in order. Unfortunately under the labour government presently in power in Great Britain I do not believe that country intends to tighten its belt. In fact in The Times of October 29 a front page heading read "Chancellor Shuns More Spending Cuts". The article following explains that because of a power play among certain members of the Labour party it is likely that the spending spree in Great Britain will continue.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I think we have come to the point where the secrecy of this government and its cavalier attitude in regard to international monetary conditions and our involvement in them, have to come to a stop. The government must accept that parliament has a right to know.
This brings me back to Clause 5 of the bill to which I referred earlier, Mr. Speaker. I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to what is the proposed substitution for Section 18(2) of the Currency and Exchange Act. Clause 5 of the bill reads as follows:
(2) An annual audit of the Exchange Fund Account and of the transactions in connection therewith shall be made by the Auditor General of Canada in such manner as he thinks proper

I hope we underline those words, Mr. Speaker.
-and he shall report to the minister and the results thereof.
That is all that will happen, Mr. Speaker. We should compare what the minister wants us to accept now with what exists in the Currency and Exchange Act, Section 18(2). Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, this wording has been in the act since it came into force in July, 1935. The present act reads:
An annual audit of the Exchange Fund Account and of the transactions in connection therewith shall be made by the Auditor General of Canada in such manner as he thinks proper-
That is where the new wording ends. The existing clause states:
-with a view to ascertaining whether the transactions in connection with the account have been in accordance with this act and he shall certify to parliament-
Mr. Speaker, please note this-not to the Minister of Finance but to parliament.
-that, in his opinion, having regard to such examination, the transactions in connection with the account have or have not been in accordance with this Act, and that the records of the account do or do not show truly and clearly the state of the account.


Currency and Exchange Act
In short, Mr. Speaker, if this bill were to pass without amendment, parliament would have lost the right to have the Auditor General report directly to us concerning transactions in the exchange fund.

subtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF THE ACT AND OTHER ACTS IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF THE ACT AND OTHER ACTS IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext:
I think there is nothing more fundamental to this parliament than our right to scrutinize such a fund and the transactions that take place. In Clause 4 of the bill we find that the Auditor General reports to the Minister of Finance. Clause 4 reads as follows:
(2) The Minister shall include the financial statements of the account and the report of the Auditor General referred to in subsection 18(2) in the report to parliament referred to in subsection (1) of this section.
Instead of having the Auditor General report directly to us on the activities within the exchange fund, the minister has very cleverly short circuited parliament. Basically he is saying, "The Auditor General reports to me, and I in turn in my regular report under the act, will include that report." That is a very different situation from the present one, Mr. Speaker. I have pointed out that Auditors General have repeatedly included in their reports to the House of Commons a special report on the exchange fund.
In the report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1975, the present Auditor General sets out at page 45 a statement of assets and liabilities for the Exchange Fund Account. I would draw this to the attention of the hon. minister. At page 46 the Auditor General makes a specific report to parliament. In short, Mr. Speaker, the present procedure is that the Auditor General makes a report not only to the Minister of Finance but also specifically a report to parliament. This is contained in his regular report to this House of Commons, a report to which we are entitled every year under the Financial Administration Act. The Auditor General acts under the provisions of the Financial Administration Act and his responsibilities are very clear. He has to report to the House of Commons concerning his findings.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that Section 18(1) of the Currency and Exchange Act shows the mischief this government is up to. That section reads:
The Financial Administration Act does not apply to the Exchange Fund Account or operations or transactions in connection therewith.
In short, Mr. Speaker, we have caught them taking advantage of the fact that under Section 18(1) the Financial Administration Act does not apply to the Currency and Exchange Act. As things now stand, Section 18(2) requires the Auditor General to report to parliament. If we pass Clause 5 of this bill, however, the Auditor General will no longer have the jurisdiction to report to this parliament because the Financial Administration Act, which he works under, does not apply to the Currency and Exchange Act. It is even questionable whether there will be any report to parliament through the public accounts, or the Auditor General's report at all. The only thing we will see will be a report presumably screened by the Minister of Finance and tabled by him in this House. We should consider the magnitude of this, Mr. Speaker. Members
[Mr. Stevens.)
of this parliament must be aroused before this bill is passed to demand an explanation of why we are asked to take away this right.
I would point out that in the Public Accounts of Canada 1976 the transactions, including the assets and liabilities of the exchange reserve accounts, are clearly set out. The exchange fund account is shown as having assets of $4 % billion. It is also set out that the foreign exchange reserve transactions in the year under review are something over $6 billion. Surely it is a very significant thing that those transactions should be properly reviewed, not merely by a screening by the Minister of Finance but by this parliament, and that we have the right to have the Auditor General continue to report to this parliament concerning his findings with regard to transactions of that magnitude.
One really should ask oneself exactly what the minister is after here. Is there something he hopes he can conceal, or does he anticipate that in the future there may be things he would just as soon not have to reveal which he would have to reveal through the reports of the Auditor General at the present time? It is very nice for the parliamentary secretary to stand up and explain that there is this provision with regard to credits and deficits over a three year period in the fund, but why should the government not be required to show the full deficit in the year in which it is incurred, or the full credit, if that is what the government is worried about. Most accounting is on the current basis. Why should there be this right to slough off the full losses we are having to live with now?
I believe there must be a serious question concerning why the bill proposes to take away from the Auditor General his responsibility which has existed since 1935 to report to this House and, second, why there is now this proposal to have this three year averaging kind of a provision. Wouldn't many businesses just love that; if there were mistakes or if they have write-offs wouldn't they love to be able to say that they do not have to report them in the immediate year but can drop them for three years!
The fact is that I believe the minister realizes we are in for a roller-coaster period and realizes he will take us more and more into the international scene where we will just have to hold on to our seats and watch the manipulations in the international monetary markets, with our commitments possibly being cut in half or to zero by countries which have to default on some of the obligations they may have to the external world. This is the reality. I believe there is no question but that we should demand that we receive full explanation and a full accounting through the Auditor General's reports right in this House and not screened through the Minister of Finance, which is what the government is cleverly trying to get through the House this evening.
The Currency and Exchange Act is an act with which most of us are quite familiar. Certainly the Bank of Canada has the immediate charge of investigating the assets of the account. I am not suggesting in any way that there is any faulty manage-


ment with regard to that account. It is well run. But I am saying that we should never at any time give up our right to have an independent Auditor General's report on those transactions in this Elouse.
In conclusion may I say it is particularly important to remember that the Auditor General in his reports over the years has been most helpful in pointing out some of the mistakes that have been made by this government. In dealing with the exchange fund the Auditor General has often pointed out that certain valuations have not been made clear and that deficits would be shown if those evaluations had been made. I refer, for example, to the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1972, and his comments in respect to the foreign exchange reserve account. Under the foreign exchange reserve accounts the advances to the exchange fund account at March 31, 1972, amounted to $5,500,000,000, comprising cash advances from the Consolidated Revenue Account of $5,146,000,000 and special drawing rights of $370 odd million. The report states:
However, as the market value of the net investments from cash advances held by the Account at that date was only $4,928,540,000, there was a deficit of $217,460,000 which in our opinion should be written off with parliamentary approval as a cost of exchange management.
That is only one of the comments. I could read into the record several that have been made by the Auditor General from time to time concerning the activities within the exchange account. If we should pass this bill in its present form it would appear that no longer would the Auditor General be required to report back to us in parliament in respect to such transactions. I would also point out that if the Financial Administration Act is not applicable, which it is not, to the Currency and Exchange Act, this means that all the rights and privileges which exist under the Financial Administration Act will not apply to the Currency and Exchange Act.
I would recommend, before we are asked to vote on this legislation, that each member carefully review the provisions of this bill and ask himself the simple question: do we want to whittle away the right we have had to have the Auditor General specifically review the activities of this fund and report back to this parliament as an obligation? Mr. Speaker, I think I should start off, initially at least, by expressing one piece of agreement with what the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) said, that it is a serious and important piece of legislation-and then we can start parting company.
I must admit that I have tremendous admiration for the self-confidence of the hon. member for York-Simcoe. Because the Canadian polls show that his party might be forming a government some time in the near future, he can hardly contain his enthusiasm and he feels he should govern Great Britain as well! I did not think that 1 would be engaging in a debate in which the shade of William Jennings Bryan and his "cross of gold" speech would be revived.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe, I think, is quite correct in his analysis when he says this is an important piece of legislation, but he might have added also that it is a very dangerous and uncertain piece of legislation, and yet the danger of acting otherwise is greater than the danger contained in this legislation.
What we are doing specifically-I suppose because it is the companion piece to the Bretton Wood's Agreement legislation-is to try to look at this bill as part of a total picture. It is an attempt on the part of the world to find some way of making sure that trade is maintained, and that countries which run into financial difficulty can be assisted without both loads of gold having to cross back and forth, or without waiting for a depression to sort things out. We have gone through that on a number of occasions. The world had bogged down completely because we were not able to devise an effective credit system in which we would help out even countries like Great Britain which had some difficulties, without suggesting that they tighten their belt before we give them any money, because what happens to Great Britain will have repercussions in this country. In the 1930's we went through the nonsense of trying to beggar our neighbour, and we destroyed each other in the process.
We have to recognize that what happens to somebody 5,000 10,000 or 15,000 miles away will ultimately affect us as well. It is a dangerous thing. There are not enough dollars around in some cases, there is not enough gold around, nor is there enough credit around. The special drawing rights have been designed as a kind of fill-in currency, perhaps some way of keeping the wheels turning and keeping things going on the basis of credit. I presume that we really do not know how well this will work out, and there is a fair amount of risk involved in dealing in this way. But 1 think this has to be done, and for that reason I am prepared to support legislation of this kind,


Currency and Exchange Act
although 1 want to raise some questions in committee and I feel that this bill should go to the committee so we can raise some questions on it there.
1 want to make a comment about Auditors General. We have had two different kinds. We have the present one, whom I admire greatly, and we have had one who seemed to be more politician than Auditor General. 1 am very curious about clause 5 of the bill. I have some reservations about the Auditor General reporting to the minister rather than to the House, but on looking at some of the preceding clauses I find that the difference between the Auditor General reporting directly to the House and reporting through the minister, who in turn reports to the House, including the financial statements of the account and the report of the Auditor General-it seems to me that basically the information the Auditor General is collecting will be made available to the House-is that there will not be any political comment in that report. By going through the minister, the Auditor General does not have to make any comment and perhaps he prefers not to make any comment on the state of the account and the values in that account because it is not really an accounting procedure that we are examining.
The minute we start dealing with such things as special drawing rights and foreign currencies and asking ourselves what valuation we place on them, it becomes a political decision and it should be dealt with as a political rather than an accounting decision, and if it is a political decision then the person to hold responsible is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) rather than the Auditor General. I say this because it seems to me that this is the only reason that I can see at the moment why the government would want to change the accounting procedure from having the Auditor General report directly to the House to having him report to the minister and then have the minister report to the House. But that is something that I will want to question and find out more about when the bill is before the committee.
There is a great danger in a bill of this kind. I am sure every member of the House recognizes that when you are dealing with currencies that are fluctuating and currencies which are not really currencies, such as special drawing rights, there is a great opportunity for hiding the cost of foreign assistance or the cost of being an international good citizen, and it will be a great problem for legislators to find out to what extent we want to bail out other countries and to what extent it will be possible to find out whether in fact we are doing it and how it is being done.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this bill, and I hope the minister or his parliamentary secretary will be able to answer some of my questions in committee.
I notice that Clause 14(2) reads:
The minister may purchase or acquire or cause to be purchased or acquired with assets held by the minister or on his behalf for the Exchange Fund Account
(a)	special drawing rights issued by the International Monetary Fund, which
rights shall be deemed for the purposes of this Part to be securities;
1 raise this because 1 think it is most important at this time in the history of the world that we have some discussion about the role of the International Monetary Fund and about world currency. Serious questions are being raised around the world and in financial circles about the effectiveness of the International Monetary Fund and how it will function.
On October 21, as reported at page 298 of Hansard, I asked the minister about the policy of the sale of gold by the International Monetary Fund which seems to be depressing the price and which has the effect, at least in this part of the world, of reducing the value of our own reserves as well as causing unemployment in our gold centres. The minister reacted by saying that in Manila he had expressed reservations about the way the gold auctions were being conducted, but that in a general way he agreed with it.
There are those who have doubts as to the ability of the International Monetary Fund to continue in the future in the way it was anticipated to operate. Perhaps the demands upon it will be much too great. There are those who argue that removing gold as one of the main ingredients in the International Monetary Fund may have been a mistake.
In committee I hope the minister will give a complete explanation of what happened in Manila and how he sees the IMF performing in the future. We have a real interest in this because according to the general economic advisory committee of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce reporting on Canada's trade and balance of payments situation from 1971 to June of 1976, since 1971 Canada's current account balance has fallen from a surplus of $431 million to a deficit of nearly $5 billion in 1975. As recently as 1973 Canada had a


small current account surplus, so in fact in two years from a small surplus we have gone to a deficit of nearly $5 billion. In the first half of 1976 the deficit was slightly higher than the same period in 1975. Although it might improve as the year goes on, there are good reasons to wonder if it will improve. Grain sales are low and prices are low at this time.
Both the merchandise and non-merchandise accounts in our trade balance showed deficits. They moved from a peak of $2.7 billion in 1973 to a deficit of $639 million in 1975. There may be a small merchandise trade surplus for this year of $500 million, as forecast by the department. But what about our deficit on non-merchandise trade? It almost doubled between 1971 and 1975 from $2.1 billion to $4.3 billion. The deficit for the first half of 1976 was about $600 million higher than for the same period in 1975. The non-merchandise deficit for the year as a whole is expected to be in the neighbourhood of $5 billion.
1 think we have a significant interest in how the IMF will function. How did this problem come about? The greatest increase has been the increase in the deficit on interest and dividends from $1.1 billion in 1971 to $2 billion in 1975. The deficit on travel rose from $200 million in 1971 to $700 million in 1975.
These are some of the very important things to be discussed with regard to this bill. Two people who are not citizens of this country spoke on this subject. One was the Prime Minister of Jamaica, Mr. Manley, and the other was the American ambassador to Canada. They talked about the problem of international payments in relation to commodity prices. I suppose they reflected the two opposite interests of this world in that Mr. Manley represented the underdeveloped countries. He talked about tyranny of trade, 20 per cent unemployment, the price of manufactured goods from industrial countries rising rapidly and the price of commodities not rising and not being fixed. On the other hand, in a speech in Edmonton Mr. Enders, the American ambassador, pointed out the great problems we have with regard to commodity prices and how they will be set. I suggest that we in Canada have not talked about commodity prices that world nations, and particularly Third World countries, desire. We have not even begun to meet their demands or to discuss their demands, although I think the ambassador, as reported in the newspapers, initiated this.
If commodity prices in the Third World are raised to a high enough level to give them a sense of security and to give them what they consider their rightful market, Canada will face importing products at a much higher price than that to which we have been accustomed.
I will close my brief remarks by pointing out the important things which are facing the world at this time. The Third World countries have debts in the amount of $40 billion or $50 billion, and there seems little hope of their being able to pay them. A few minutes ago on television we saw an interview with Mr. Carter, the President-elect of the United States, with regard to what he would be able to do if the OPEC nations raised their price of oil by 20 per cent. His answer was that he did not hold out much hope that there would be very much
Currency and Exchange Act
which could be done. The United Kingdom is asking for $3.9 billion from the International Monetary Fund, and Mexico has just negotiated a loan of nearly $1 billion. It is now thought that the IMF does not have enough resources to cover even those loans, which are probably small compared with the demands which will be made on the IMF in the future.
In committee I hope we can get from the minister some idea of how he thinks the IMF will cope with the world situation and how he sees Canada's role in the IMF, which is a matter touched upon in this bill.

Mr. Speaker, we are discussing this evening some amendments to a legislation, which according to the text can be entitled: The Currency and Exchange Act. On the other hand, what is suggested? Some amendments are proposed and according to the explanatory notes, I see in clause I that we will add to the currencies considered in Canadian contracts some units of account such as the special drawing rights issued by the International Monetary Fund.
Mr. Speaker, we have discussed at great length in previous years other bills dealing with the benefits of special drawing rights. However, I regret very much that this afternoon when the Minister made his statement on the bill, he refused to explain the benefits for Canada of those special drawing rights issued by the International Monetary Fund.
I have had some experience of what the Government of Canada had to contend with in the IMF. I am reminded of what happened in 1968, and what happened further back, in 1962, when I think of the problems Canada encountered in its participation in the IMF. 1 do not regret those experiences the Government of Canada underwent. I remember, in the name of international monetary sanity, and I underline sanity, the rebuke or, shall we say, the "Cry halt" which was imposed on the Government of Canada at that time. One must bear in mind the difficulties of interpreting certain statistical information and the fact that various countries, not always the same ones, behaved in a rather strange manner over the years.
I think of what happened to the Government of Canada of the 1962 epoch, when the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert was Prime Minister, and what happened in 1968 when the Right Hon. Lester Pearson was Prime Minister. The latter had to cut short a holiday in Jamaica by reason of the most horrendous international financial bind Canada had ever known. I may say that in the spirit of the crisis then facing Canada-and it is well known that the Liberal administration of the time was defeated on the third reading of an income tax bill-the then Prime Minister who had to cut short his holiday in Jamaica asked the then leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), to give the government 24 hours' respite. And the hon. member for Halifax, with his intense loyalty to Canada, of which I know and which cannot


Currency and Exchange Act
be measured, agreed; because to him, and to me, were exposed the positions of the international financial account at the time.
We could have mounted an offensive to defeat the government; but it would have been a Pyrrhic victory. Many of those lusting for blood and many bloodsuckers, whether they were social scientists, newspaper columnists, or just plain Bob Stanfield haters, said that the hon. member for Halifax was too soft on that occasion. Mr. Speaker, I want to be on record as saying that Bob Stanfield at that time acted for Canada. There are no two ways about it. Sure, he could have carried on a guerrilla campaign within this House which might have had the support of the NDP and the Creditiste party, and particularly of the Creditiste party of that time, against a motion of general support for the government. But you know, Mr. Speaker, at that time Canada had reached the most perilous international financial status it had ever known.
To meet Canada's trade requirements and those of other countries as well, there was devised a system of international finance. Canada has no particular formula, nor particular pride of possession in this regard. Some trading partners with whom we are proud to deal run into difficulty from time to time. I am sure that all members of the House share with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) the hope that somehow, over the years, we will so arrange our mutual affairs internationally as to avoid unnecessary international dislocations. This will not necessarily be done under this bill, in the case of Canada, or under another bill to amend the Bretton Woods Agreement.
Internationally we have had some rough passages in the past. We are going to have some really bumpy passages to negotiate in the next few years. In this regard I refer hon. members to a speech I made the other day on Bill C-15 with regard to the customs tariff. As I, and my colleague from York-Simcoe, and others in the House will show, in international trade this country is going to negotiate some really bumpy water. In his heart I think the minister agrees.
Having said that I say to the minister, and I am sure colleagues on my side of the House agree, that we will participate in any positive measure, if it is going to smooth the rough water ahead which Canadian trade must negotiate during the next few years. And when one speaks of Canadian trade one immediately says, "Yes, but the condition of our trade is reflected in the value of Canadian currency." Mr. Speaker, as I recall, a couple of years ago we went through the exercise of establishing special drawing rights. The minister is asking us to accept an amendment in Clause 1 of the bill, which is quite reasonable I think, to this effect: that in a contract, if there are to be certain, shall we say, equivalents expressed as between Canadian currency and a foreign currency, they may also be expressed in SDRs. I think that is perfectly legitimate. But there are other things which the minister must explain.
Within the general philosophy of this bill there is a greater concentration of ministerial interpretation which is for the

benefit of the government. Let us look at an example in the language of the bill. Clause 14(2) reads:
The Minister may purchase or acquire or cause to be purchased or acquired with assets held by the Minister or on his behalf for the Exchange Fund Account
I simply raise the question, why? A little further on there is a change in the language where it reads:
(b)	currency of the United States, deposits in currency of the United States held in the name of the Minister with the Bank of Canada or any bank designated by the Minister and securities of the United States;
When we look at the previous act again we say why?
(c)	such currencies as the Minister designates as freely usable currencies-
In the past it read:
(c) currencies of any country other than Canada or the United States that are freely convertible into gold or United States dollars;
Why is the designation of the minister introduced?
I then come to the point that was made by my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). Notwithstanding my general disposition to amendments to the act to make it more administratively feasible, I cry halt. In Section 5 the Minister of Finance says that any examination of the Foreign Exchange Fund Account shall be submitted to him by the Auditor General. That is the point of no return. The Auditor General and his role have been the subject of a great deal of discussion in this House, in newspaper editorials and in academic circles. On this particular point I would defy any member on the government side of the House, from the minister down to the newest backbencher, to debate with me and my colleagues any reason why there should not be a straight, uncomplicated, and direct report on this account from the Auditor General to the Parliament of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, October 22, as recorded in Hansard at page 368, I put a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) regarding Heritage Day. In particular I asked him if the report of last session was true, namely, that at this session there would be a comprehensive holidays bill which the government would introduce and which would include Heritage Day in the month of February. The minister's answer to that question was a categorical yes. That answer was very satisfactory, and


Adjournment Debate
therefore the minister may wonder why I am raising the matter on a late show.
The reason, of course, is to be found in the answer he gave to my supplementary question. In my supplementary question I asked him whether action could be taken in time so that the first Heritage Day could be celebrated in February, 1977. His reply was to the effect that he hoped that would be the case, but he could not promise it.
The reason I am here tonight-and at this hour of the night those of us on the late show will have enough sense to shorten our questions-is to give the minister a chance to revise that answer. Surely if it has been decided by the government that Heritage Day is to be added to the list of holidays in Canada, there is no reason to delay it for another year.
Actually when Mr. Justice Emmett Hall dealt with a railway dispute well over two years ago, the possibility of Heritage Day becoming a holiday was then before us, and he gave the railway workers at that time reason to believe that the contract he was settling for them would include Heritage Day. They have missed two of them; surely they are not going to miss another.
1 believe the idea of a Heritage Day is a good one in terms of what it would recognize, and it is a good idea in this country to have a holiday in February. I was glad that the minister said the other day that the government agrees. I hope tonight he can make a short answer and say that the bill will be introduced in time so that we can celebrate the first Heritage Day in February, 1977.

NATIONAL DEFENCE-FAILURE TO REINSTATE WILLIAM BIGGS-REQUEST FOR INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Mr. William Biggs, a retired army captain having served 25 years with the Canadian forces, was from 1970 to 1974 a civilian employed by Canadian Forces Europe, holding the position of manager of the automobile transaction office in Lahr, Germany. In November, 1974, Biggs without warning was locked out of his office and suspended. He was accused by the Canadian forces of, among other things, fraud, misappropriation of funds, and falsification of accounts. On December 20, 1974, he was fired.
On December 1 of that year while still under suspension Biggs wrote to the Commander, Canadian Forces Europe, requesting a military hearing and access to the ATO files in order to prove his innocence. From that time he has written numerous letters of grievance to his military superiors; to date none of them have been answered except by form acknowledgments of receipt. He was, however, told in February, 1975, by Major General Quinn, Commander of CFE, in answer to a point by point rebuttal written by Biggs, that Biggs' redress of grievance would be answered when the investigation was complete. Nothing further has been heard from General Quinn except that in a letter to Mrs. Biggs, in response to an appeal on her husband's behalf, General Quinn stated that he considered the matter closed.


Immediately after being suspended, a radio announcement was made on the Canadian radio station that the ATO office was closed temporarily due to the results of an audit showing certain discrepancies in its books. The entire community in Lahr was, and still is, under the impression that Mr. Biggs was caught with his hand in the till. In truth there was no audit made before that time. The special investigation unit of the Canadian forces investigated the charges against Mr. Biggs and turned their reports over to the German civil authorities. Mr. Biggs was prosecuted in a German court. On January 27, 1976, his case was heard in the Lahr county court. He was acquitted of all charges against him, and in addition the judge said:
In the course of the hearing the accused has proven himself to be a man of honour, whose seriousness and integrity are not doubted, the reproaches that were raised against him have proven to be absolutely unfounded.
Even the state prosecutor, after he had heard some of his own evidence, requested a dismissal of the charges. The evidence was taken and the case dismissed. Mr. Biggs, of course, expected to be reinstated if found innocent, but this has not happened, and he has instead been informed that the military consider the case closed.
The conduct of this case involves many disturbing and unjust procedures. At no time was he given a clear statement of the allegations against him. The letter of termination includes four paragraphs of charges; these paragraphs state that he did certain things either dishonestly or negligently, but they do not specify the exact transactions referred to and are extremely vague with respect to his exact offences. One of the reasons for this vagueness is undoubtedly that although the letter suggests he may have been dishonest, dishonesty is a ground for firing an employee in Biggs' position only if it is admitted or proven. As it was, neither of the allegations was framed as "unsatisfactory work performance."
Letter after letter from the military personnel stated that his grievance could not be dealt with until the Germans had completed their case against him. Yet no one from the Canadian forces was present at the German trial and, after its completion, no action was taken in response to Mr. Biggs' letter of grievance.
In conclusion, the letter of termination of December, 1974, indicates that Mr. Biggs was either dishonest-and he was entirely cleared of charges of dishonesty by a German county court-or grossly negligent. If in fact Mr. Biggs was incompetent, one would have thought that it might have been discovered some time in his 25 years of military service, or in his four years' service with the automobile transaction office, rather than in the middle of an investigation resulting in trumped up charges which were dismissed in court. In addition, the way in which Mr. Biggs was fired left a cloud hanging over his head. His reputation in the community in which he lives is now that of a dishonest man, and he has for the last two years been unable to find another job. The destruction of a man's reputation and of his ability to earn a livelihood surely requires that he have the opportunity at the
Adjournment Debate
very least to answer specific allegations and a chance to restore his good name.
Mr. Biggs has been tried and found innocent but, despite this, has been savagely punished. This is a travesty of basic Canadian justice and fair play.
I point out to the minister that the Canadian Bill of Rights
states, in Part I:
... no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to ... deprive a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations.
To illustrate how fundamental the justice is which is being denied to Mr. Biggs, I also point out that Magna Carta states:
No free man shall be seized . .. nor will we condemn him ... excepting by the legal judgment of his peers, or by the laws of the land.
The minister is new at this job, up until now I have always considered him a fair man. I am aware that there has been a "closing of the ranks" on this subject in his department where, of course, the only advice he can get is from the people who instituted or confirmed this outrageous course of action. I have made available to the minister a very brief summation of the facts, as obtained by an independent source. It is now up to him to show the stuff he is made of and to institute an independent inquiry into this very disturbing matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice A. Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-FAILURE TO REINSTATE WILLIAM BIGGS-REQUEST FOR INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has asked me to thank the hon. member for his interest in the case. I wish to assure the hon. member that the minister is personally investigating the matter. I am sure the hon. member will appreciate that the minister has been in charge of the department only for a couple of days and obviously has not had chance to investigate all documents and facts pertinent to the case. The minister would also wish me to thank the hon. member for making available to him a summary of the facts, which he mentioned a few moments ago, facts which he will want to examine closely.
The hon. member himself used expressions such as "disturbing aspects", "trumped-up charges", savagely punished" and "travesty of justice". If such terms represent the feelings of the hon. member and of Mr. Biggs, then it is all the more important for the minister to look carefully at the case, if he is to make a fair and honest determination. The minister has authorized me to assure the hon. member that after he has had an opportunity of reviewing the entire case, he will report his findings to the hon. member personally.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXFANSION-REASON FOR FAILURE TO MAKE CHANGES TO INCENTIVES ACT
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXFANSION-REASON FOR FAILURE TO MAKE CHANGES TO INCENTIVES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the second or third day of the present session of parliament I raised a question concerning possible amendments to the Regional Development Incentives Act. Numerous suggestions have been made by advisory bodies to the minister, by provincial governments, and other independent bodies with respect to this particular act.


Adjournment Debate
One would have expected to have seen in the recent Speech from the Throne an indication that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion had been dealing in specific terms with some of the improvements and modifications that many Canadians now feel will be necessary if the basic task of assisting and developing industry in regions of economic and social disparity is to be accomplished.
Frankly I was surprised in the first instance that there was no reference in the Speech from the Throne to this matter. 1 was even more surprised and disturbed when I raised the question in the Elouse on October 13 with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard). In his answer with regard to the lack of any indication in the Speech from the Throne and whether there was any recommendation to his cabinet colleagues on this matter and whether they had turned it down, the minister said, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, no recommendations have actually been made to cabinet at this point by myself or my department because we are now considering as we have done in recent weeks several representations made by various Canadian organizations on the ways to amend the act. I do hope that in the months to come we will be able to reach a consensus in that respect. I would then be in a position to submit to my colleagues in cabinet the amendments that will prove appropriate to meet the needs.
I find this a disturbing answer from a minister who represents a department that claims to be specifically interested in and charged with the problems of economic and social disparity in the various regions of the country.
I realize that the Regional Development Incentives Act is not the major component in the expenditures of this department. It occupies only 20 per cent or less of the department's budget. Much of the money goes into the kind of infrastructure programs that are under the general development agreement and subsidiary agreements with the various provinces.
What is disturbing is that the recommendations that have been made for some time now have virtually been ignored to this date by the minister and his officials. Since 1973 the minister has had a draft report from the Atlantic Development Council. It was published this year. I quote from the report:
The evidence to date and the trends with respect to offers and applications suggest that unless significant changes in policy and its applications are made, the program as far as the Atlantic region is concerned will not achieve further momentum, but on the contrary, may significantly run down.
The minister has had that advice before him, presumably, for three years. It is not the only report that has been made available to the minister, first from his own advisory group and also from independent studies, some of which have been considered by the regional development committee of this House. The ADC report went on to say, and I quote:
As a result of RDIA in Atlantic Canada, 'an average of only one new project per year had entered commercial production in the region that possibly would have located elsewhere'.
In addition, major concern has been expressed by independent studies and members on both sides of this House with regard to the amount of ministerial discretion and latitude that exists concerning the approval of project applications.
As far back as June 20, 1972, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) asked for the expedition of grants and
(Mr. MacDonald (Egmont).]
demanded less completed work before making payment. Indeed the Liberal party policy convention in 1975 called for the elimination of DREE red tape. There are a number of points that have been made. There is not time this evening to quote all of them.
On December 5, 1975, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) suggested RDIA should not use uniform standards across the country. The Canadian Council on Rural Development, an advisory body to the minister, in 1969, as well as the Atlantic Development Council in its report published this year, called for more industrial intelligence and post-incentive assistance.
Of greater importance, however, are suggestions that have been made not only by advisory bodies but by provincial governments with regard to the universal coverage of RDIA. Concern has been expressed from the outset.
I recall being a member of the regional development committee in 1969 reviewing the initial legislation and being concerned about the application of this act to service industries. Representations have certainly been made by provincial governments and, in one instance, by the four ministers of tourism in the Atlantic provinces with respect to the importance of RDIA amendments in relation to the tourist industry. In addition, the former minister of regional economic expansion, now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), indicated there might well be three or four amendments dealing with bridge financing, a matter of great importance in the establishment of new industries in economically deprived areas.
I suppose that in the short time available to me I should draw attention to what is a major concern of those of us who have been studying the effects of this act, that is, the difficulty of defining an effective goal and strategy with respect to the federal program of industrial assistance. The Atlantic Council, in a recent report, has stated that from the outset there has never been a clearly defined industrial strategy to which the RDIA would apply. This view was expressed also in a number of independent studies. After seven years it is far too late for the minister to tell us that the government has just begun to study recommendations which have been well-known for years. It is high time some action was taken and it is my hope that the government will act to bring about long overdue amendments to the Regional Development Incentives Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ed Lumley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXFANSION-REASON FOR FAILURE TO MAKE CHANGES TO INCENTIVES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 was pleased to note from the question asked during the queston period on October 13 by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) that he recognizes the importance of the Regional Development Incentives Act as a tool for implementing regional development policy. This is a view which I personally share with him and one which is held by many other groups as well, including provincial governments and the Atlantic Development Council.


In his question the other day the hon. member referred to recommendations made by the Atlantic Development Council as an advisory body to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard). I assume he is referring specifically to the recommendations contained in a study published by the Council in May, 1976, which relates to activity under the program during the period from 1969 to 1972.
That study did indeed make recommendations for improving the effectiveness of the regional development incentives program. There are, however, two important points that I would like to make in this regard.
First, the council noted that-and 1 quote from the report:
"The incentives program in the Atlantic region has been a useful source of financial assistance for industry and has brought a welcome contribution to the growth of employment".
Therefore, even on the basis of early and limited experience with the program, the council study revealed that the program was proving effective.
Second, and perhaps more important, the Council recognized in its report that its recommendations had been "taken into account in the formulation of a number of changes in departmental administration and in the operation of the RD1A program itself." In other words, the council recognized that the department had, on its own initiative, undertaken a policy review of the regional development incentives program and had adopted many of the changes proposed by other bodies including provincial governments and the Atlantic Development Council itself. The decentralization of decision-making and the introduction of standard formulae for certain types of incentives projects are two examples of the recommendations made by the council which were adopted by the department.
Adjournment Debate
Although this major review of the incentives program was undertaken in 1972 and 1973 and changes were initiated in 1974, this is not to say that we are now content with the program and will make no further changes to improve its effectiveness. In fact, as my minister said the other day in response to the question from the hon. Member for Egmont, we are constantly reviewing the on-going operation of the incentives program and continually considering ways and means by which it can be made a better tool for fostering economic expansion and social adjustment in disadvantaged regions of the country.
In this regard, it will be remembered that only last year parliament approved an extension to the act from 1976 to 1981. That extension permits the continued provision of incentives to industry of all sizes, including small businesses where increased emphasis was made possible as a result of the program changes in 1974. It will also provide an opportunity to consider the representations of various Canadian groups and to determine how the government's and the department's objectives can best be met and what, if any, amendments to the Regional Development Incentives Act will be required during that period.
I hope these remarks will help to clarify for all concerned the actions taken recently by our department in relation to the incentives program and our intentions with regard to this program in the future.
